For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

derivations.claim: If $z=0$, the claim is equality. For $z<0$, fix any $a<b\le0$ and set $g(t)=1+t-\exp(t)$. By [F2], $g'(t)=1-\exp(t)\ge0$ for $t\le0$, because [F3] and [F1] give $\exp(t)\le\exp(0)=1$. Applying [F4] to $g$ on $[a,b]$ shows $g(b)-g(a)=g'(c)(b-a)\ge0$, so $g$ is nondecreasing on $(-\infty,0]$.

Now $g(0)=0$, so step 1.1 gives $g(t)\le0$ for every $t\le0$. Set $f(t)=1+t+t^2/2-\exp(t)$; then $f'(t)=g(t)$. Applying [F4] on $[z,0]$ gives $f(0)-f(z)=g(c)(-z)\le0$. Since $f(0)=0$, $f(z)\ge0$, which is the required inequality.

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

derivations.claim: Fix a positive-probability atom $H$ of the finite pre-action history. On $H$, $y_{t,i}$ and $P_{t,i}$ are fixed. By [F1], $\mathbb P(H\cap\{A_t=i\})=P_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)$; the estimator is $y_{t,i}/P_{t,i}$ on that event and zero on the rest of $H$. Hence $\int_H\widehat Y_{t,i}\,d\mathbb P=y_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)$. The function with value $y_{t,i}$ on each history atom is measurable and integrable, and finite additivity gives the same integral identity on every event in $\mathcal F_{t-1}$. By [F2], it is a conditional-expectation version, proving $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}$.

On the same atom $H$, $\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}$ is $y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}^2$ on $H\cap\{A_t=i\}$ and zero otherwise. Thus $\int_H\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}\,d\mathbb P=(y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}^2)P_{t,i}\mathbb P(H)=(y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i})\mathbb P(H)$. Extending over the finite atoms and applying [F2] proves $\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{\,2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i}^2/P_{t,i}$.

At a fixed history, the centered estimator has value $y_{t,i}(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}$ with probability $P_{t,i}$ and value $-y_{t,i}$ with probability $1-P_{t,i}$, by step 1.1. Its conditional variance is therefore $P_{t,i}[y_{t,i}(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}]^2+(1-P_{t,i})y_{t,i}^2=y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})/P_{t,i}$.

citations.quote: In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The output is $(P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widehat Y_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $\widehat S_n$. These operations use exact real arithmetic. The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge.

In the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition, fix a round $t$ and arm $i$, and write $p=P_{t,i}>0$ and $y=y_{t,i}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i},\qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\frac{y_{t,i}^2}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
With conditional variance defined by $\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}])^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, one also has
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\frac{y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})}{P_{t,i}}.
$$

For every real $z\le0$,
$$
\exp(z)\le1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}.
$$

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,

2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then

3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class only if there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

In the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition, fix a round $t$ and arm $i$, and write $p=P_{t,i}>0$ and $y=y_{t,i}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=y_{t,i},\qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Y_{t,i}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\frac{y_{t,i}^2}{P_{t,i}}.
$$
With conditional variance defined by $\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}])^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$, one also has
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=\frac{y_{t,i}^2(1-P_{t,i})}{P_{t,i}}.
$$

Since $\widehat X_{1,1}=1-\widehat Y_{1,1}$, its values are $-9$ and $1$ on the two events, respectively, so it can fall outside the true reward range $[0,1]$.

routine_steps.claim: Since $\widehat S_{0,1}=\widehat S_{0,2}=0$, Exp3 starts with probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$. If $A_1=1$, then $Y_1=0$ and $\widehat X_{1,1}=\widehat X_{1,2}=1$, so the next Exp3 distribution is uniform. If $A_1=2$, then $Y_1=1$, $P_{1,2}=1/2$, and $(\widehat Y_{1,1},\widehat Y_{1,2})=(0,2)$; hence $\widehat X_1=(1,-1)$ and the next distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)),\exp(-\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)))$.
Full-information Hedge uses $\epsilon=\eta$ and sees losses $(0,1)$, so its next weights are $(1,\exp(-\eta))$ and its normalized distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+1),1/(\exp(\eta)+1))$.

By [F4] and [F6], $\exp(\eta)>1$, so Hedge's first probability exceeds $1/2$ and differs from Exp3's first probability after $A_1=1$. Also $\exp(2\eta)>\exp(\eta)$, so the odds ratio after $A_1=2$ is $\exp(2\eta)$ for Exp3 and $\exp(\eta)$ for Hedge; these distributions differ as well.
